slides.body: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
Three parts. Events and filters: which commit and ref a run is about, which copy of the workflow file is used, and how a branch or path filter decides whether a run is created at all.
The path filter part has a local demonstration, because the comparison GitHub documents is a plain Git diff, and you can run it before pushing.
Here's what you'll walk away with.

slides.body: Before the push, the lab asks you to predict: which workflows start for the pull request, and how many checks will it show?
Five mistakes to watch for.

items: A required check on a workflow with a paths filter. Root cause: a workflow that a filter skips never creates its check, and the ruleset waits for a result that will not come.
Predicting a pull request path filter with a two-dot diff. Root cause: for pull requests the comparison is three dots, from the merge base; two dots include what changed on the base branch.
An if with text outside the expression wrapper. Root cause: the whole value becomes a non-empty string, which is truthy, so the condition is always true.
A typing error in steps.<id>.outputs. Root cause: a property that does not exist evaluates to an empty string, without an error.
Expecting a secret in a fork pull request, or testing secrets in if. Root cause: secrets are not passed to workflows triggered from forks, and the secrets context is not available in if.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. In the last video you learned the model, and a reading order that starts with the trigger. Now you learn to read the trigger properly, and then two more things that sit between the trigger and your commands.

beats.text: Three parts. Events and filters: which commit and ref a run is about, which copy of the workflow file is used, and how a branch or path filter decides whether a run is created at all. Contexts and expressions: the data a workflow can read and the small formula language over it, with the question that matters most, which is when an expression is evaluated. And env, vars and secrets: three things that look alike in a script and differ in where they're defined and who can read them.

And `env`, `vars` and `secrets`: three things that look alike in a script and differ in where they're defined and who can read them.

beats.text: Events. In one sentence: the on key lists the events that start a run. Each event fixes which commit and ref the run is about and which copy of the workflow file is used. A ref is a name such as a branch or a tag. And filters narrow an event to branches, tags or paths.

beats.text: on takes one event, a list, or a map from event to its configuration. The textbook lists eight events with the values the events reference gives for GITHUB_SHA and GITHUB_REF. Take the four you'll meet first.

beats.text: push starts when commits or tags are pushed. The commit is the tip commit pushed to the ref. The ref is the updated ref. It runs for any branch, including workflows not merged into the default branch.
beats.tele: `push` starts when commits or tags are pushed. The commit is the tip commit pushed to the ref. The ref is the updated ref. It runs for any branch, including workflows not merged into the default branch.

beats.text: pull_request starts when a pull request is opened, gets new commits, or is reopened. Other activity types need types. The commit is the last merge commit on the GITHUB_REF branch, and the ref is refs/pull/N/merge. That's the test merge that GitHub computes for the pull request. So the commit isn't the tip of your branch. Video 145 is about that. And the reference adds: it doesn't run while the pull request has a merge conflict.

So the commit isn't the tip of your branch. Video 145 is about that. And the reference adds: it doesn't run while the pull request has a merge conflict.

beats.text: workflow_dispatch starts when someone starts it by hand, with the CLI or the API. The commit is the last commit on the chosen branch or tag, and the ref is that branch or tag. It works only if the workflow file exists on the default branch.
beats.tele: `workflow_dispatch` starts when someone starts it by hand, with the CLI or the API. The commit is the last commit on the chosen branch or tag, and the ref is that branch or tag. It works only if the workflow file exists on the default branch.

beats.text: schedule starts when a cron expression matches. The commit is the last commit on the default branch. The ref is the default branch. It's in UTC unless a timezone is given. The shortest interval is five minutes. It can be delayed or dropped under load. And in a public repository it is disabled after 60 days without repository activity.

beats.text: Filters. push accepts filters for branches, tags and paths, each with an -ignore form. pull_request accepts the branch filters, which match the base branch, and the two path filters. Four rules.
beats.tele: Filters. `push` accepts filters for branches, tags and paths, each with an `-ignore` form. `pull_request` accepts the branch filters, which match the base branch, and the two path filters. Four rules.

beats.text: A positive filter and an -ignore filter of the same kind can't be combined for one event. You use an exclamation mark pattern inside the positive filter, and order matters.
beats.tele: A positive filter and an `-ignore` filter of the same kind can't be combined for one event. You use an exclamation mark pattern inside the positive filter, and order matters.

beats.text: When a branch filter and a path filter are both present, the workflow runs only when both are satisfied.
beats.tele: When a branch filter and a path filter are both present, the workflow runs only when both are satisfied.

beats.text: Path filters aren't evaluated for pushes of tags.
beats.tele: Path filters aren't evaluated for pushes of tags.

beats.text: And the rule the demonstration is built on: path filters compare with a three-dot diff for pull requests and a two-dot diff for pushes. Two limits come with it. A push with more than 1,000 commits, or a diff that times out, always runs the workflow. A diff of more than 3,000 files in which the match isn't among the first 3,000 doesn't.

A push with more than 1,000 commits, or a diff that times out, always runs the workflow. A diff of more than 3,000 files in which the match isn't among the first 3,000 doesn't.

beats.text: Two more ways a run doesn't come to exist. A commit whose message contains [skip ci], or one of its documented variants, skips push and pull_request workflows. And events created by a workflow's own job token don't start new workflow runs, with documented exceptions: workflow_dispatch, repository_dispatch, and pull request events, which wait for approval since the eleventh of June 2026. So a job that pushes a commit with the job token doesn't trigger the push workflows for that commit.

And events created by a workflow's own job token don't start new workflow runs, with documented exceptions: `workflow_dispatch`, `repository_dispatch`, and pull request events, which wait for approval since the eleventh of June 2026. So a job that pushes a commit with the job token doesn't trigger the `push` workflows for that commit.

beats.text: Contexts and expressions. In one sentence: a context is a named object of facts about the run, and an expression, written with a dollar sign and double braces, is a small formula over contexts that GitHub Actions replaces with its value before your step starts.
beats.tele: Contexts and expressions. In one sentence: a context is a named object of facts about the run, and an expression, written with a dollar sign and double braces, is a small formula over contexts that GitHub Actions replaces with its value before your step starts.

beats.text: The contexts you'll use first: github, with the event name, the full event payload, the ref, the commit, the actor and the run numbers. env. vars. secrets. inputs. matrix. steps, which holds the outputs and outcome of earlier steps that have an id. And needs, which holds the outputs and result of the jobs listed in needs.
beats.tele: The contexts you'll use first: `github`, with the event name, the full event payload, the ref, the commit, the actor and the run numbers. `env`. `vars`. `secrets`. `inputs`. `matrix`. `steps`, which holds the outputs and outcome of earlier steps that have an `id`. And `needs`, which holds the outputs and result of the jobs listed in `needs`.

beats.text: The rules of the expression language that cause surprises.
beats.tele: The rules of the expression language that cause surprises.

beats.text: Strings use single quotes inside the braces. Double quotes are an error.
beats.tele: Strings use single quotes inside the braces. Double quotes are an error.

beats.text: String comparison ignores case. When the two sides of an equality differ in type, both are converted to numbers.
beats.tele: String comparison ignores case. When the two sides of an equality differ in type, both are converted to numbers.

beats.text: A property that doesn't exist evaluates to an empty string, without an error. A typing error in the name of a step ID is therefore silent.
beats.tele: A property that doesn't exist evaluates to an empty string, without an error. A typing error in the name of a step ID is therefore silent.

beats.text: The functions include contains, startsWith, format, toJSON, fromJSON, hashFiles, and the status functions success(), failure(), cancelled() and always(). The function case has existed since the twenty-ninth of January 2026. Older files imitate it with "condition and a, or b", which returns b whenever a is falsy.

The function `case` has existed since the twenty-ninth of January 2026. Older files imitate it with "condition and a, or b", which returns b whenever a is falsy.

beats.text: Context availability is per key. A job-level if can read github, needs, vars and inputs, but not matrix, steps, env or secrets. A step-level if can read matrix, steps and env, but still not secrets. The reason is timing: a job-level if is decided before a runner exists, so nothing that lives on the runner can take part.
beats.tele: Context availability is per key. A job-level `if` can read `github`, `needs`, `vars` and `inputs`, but not `matrix`, `steps`, `env` or `secrets`. A step-level `if` can read `matrix`, `steps` and `env`, but still not `secrets`. The reason is timing: a job-level `if` is decided before a runner exists, so nothing that lives on the runner can take part.

beats.text: The trap in if. The wrapper of dollar sign and braces is optional in an if, unless the expression starts with an exclamation mark. Text outside the wrapper turns the whole value into a non-empty string, which is truthy. The condition is then always true.

beats.text: env, vars and secrets. In one sentence: env is defined in the workflow file and becomes environment variables of the process. vars and secrets are stored in GitHub settings and are read through contexts. Only secrets are encrypted and masked.
beats.tele: `env`, `vars` and `secrets`. In one sentence: `env` is defined in the workflow file and becomes environment variables of the process. `vars` and `secrets` are stored in GitHub settings and are read through contexts. Only `secrets` are encrypted and masked.

beats.text: Where each is defined: env in the workflow file, at workflow, job or step level. vars and secrets in the settings of the organization, the repository or an environment.
beats.tele: Where each is defined: `env` in the workflow file, at workflow, job or step level. `vars` and `secrets` in the settings of the organization, the repository or an environment.

beats.text: Who can see it: env is in the file. vars aren't in the repository but readable in settings and logs. secrets are write-only in settings.
beats.tele: Who can see it: `env` is in the file. `vars` aren't in the repository but readable in settings and logs. `secrets` are write-only in settings.

beats.text: How it reaches a step: env as an environment variable. vars and secrets only through their context. You map them into env, or for a secret into env or with.
beats.tele: How it reaches a step: `env` as an environment variable. `vars` and `secrets` only through their context. You map them into `env`, or for a secret into `env` or `with`.

beats.text: Precedence for the same name: for env, the most specific wins, step over job over workflow. For vars, environment over repository over organization. For secrets, the environment-level secret wins.
beats.tele: Precedence for the same name: for `env`, the most specific wins, step over job over workflow. For `vars`, environment over repository over organization. For secrets, the environment-level secret wins.

beats.text: Masking: env no, vars no, secrets yes, when the exact value appears. The textbook adds three words: not a guarantee.
beats.tele: Masking: `env` no, `vars` no, `secrets` yes, when the exact value appears. The textbook adds three words: not a guarantee.

beats.text: Quick quiz. A deploy step reads a secret that nobody ever set. What does the step receive? A, an error that stops the run. B, an empty string. Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz. A deploy step reads a secret that nobody ever set. What does the step receive? A, an error that stops the run. B, an empty string. Your answer?

beats.text: B, an empty string. Three behaviors cause real failures. An unset secret is an empty string, not an error. A deploy step that receives an empty credential fails later and elsewhere, with a message about authentication. Secrets aren't passed to workflows triggered from forks or by Dependabot, apart from a read-only job token.

A deploy step that receives an empty credential fails later and elsewhere, with a message about authentication. Secrets aren't passed to workflows triggered from forks or by Dependabot, apart from a read-only job token.

beats.text: A fork is a second repository on GitHub, made from the first. A fork pull request that "fails only in CI" is often a job that needed a secret. And secrets can't be used in if. You map the secret into env and test whether the variable is non-empty.

beats.text: GITHUB_TOKEN is a secret that GitHub creates for each job. What it may do is set by the permissions key, and when any permission is named, every unnamed one becomes none.
beats.tele: `GITHUB_TOKEN` is a secret that GitHub creates for each job. What it may do is set by the `permissions` key, and when any permission is named, every unnamed one becomes none.

beats.text: Analogy, from the textbook. An expression is a mail-merge field. The letter, which is your step, is printed with the field already filled in. The recipient, which is the shell, never sees the field, only the text.

beats.text: The textbook says the analogy is exact about the danger and incomplete about the timing. Exact about the danger: text substituted into a script becomes part of the script. That's how an untrusted pull request title becomes a shell command, and video 158 is about that. Incomplete about the timing: not every field is available in every place.

beats.text: So for every expression ask: who evaluates this, and when? There are three moments.
beats.tele: So for every expression ask: who evaluates this, and when? There are three moments.

beats.text: On the runner, per step, before the shell starts, the step-level if, with, env, and any expression inside a run text are evaluated.
beats.tele: On the runner, per step, before the shell starts, the step-level `if`, `with`, `env`, and any expression inside a `run` text are evaluated.

beats.text: And at run time, the shell expands an ordinary shell variable.
beats.tele: And at run time, the shell expands an ordinary shell variable.

beats.text: The difference between the last two is a security boundary. An expression inside run pastes the value into the script text. A value mapped into env and then read as a shell variable is handed to the shell as data. Every course workflow uses the second form, including for values that aren't attacker-controlled, so that the habit is uniform.

beats.text: Read the trigger of workflows/02-lint.yml first: pushes to main, and pull requests. The lab has you add the workflow on a branch named ci/lint, push the branch and open a pull request. git push is 🟡 CAUTION and gh pr create is 🟡 CAUTION: it creates a GitHub object that notifies people.
beats.tele: Read the trigger of `workflows/02-lint.yml` first: pushes to `main`, and pull requests. The lab has you add the workflow on a branch named `ci/lint`, push the branch and open a pull request. `git push` is 🟡 CAUTION and `gh pr create` is 🟡 CAUTION: it creates a GitHub object that notifies people.

beats.text: Before the push, the lab asks you to predict: which workflows start for the pull request, and how many checks will it show? Think about it with what you know. The push to ci/lint is a push, but not to main, so the push trigger with its branch filter doesn't match. The pull_request trigger matches once the pull request exists. And the lint workflow file is on the branch, not yet on main: for pull_request, which copy is used?
beats.tele: Before the push, the lab asks you to predict: which workflows start for the pull request, and how many checks will it show? Think about it with what you know. The push to `ci/lint` is a push, but not to `main`, so the `push` trigger with its branch filter doesn't match. The `pull_request` trigger matches once the pull request exists. And the lint workflow file is on the branch, not yet on `main`: for `pull_request`, which copy is used?

beats.text: In the browser, open the pull request and find the list of checks. Name each by the workflow and job it comes from. Then look at two expressions in the file while the run is in progress: the if with !cancelled() on the formatting step, which needs the wrapper because it starts with an exclamation mark, and the summary step that maps two step outcomes into env before the shell reads them.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: A required check on a workflow with a paths filter. Root cause: a workflow that a filter skips never creates its check, and the ruleset waits for a result that will not come.
beats.tele: A required check on a workflow with a `paths` filter. Root cause: a workflow that a filter skips never creates its check, and the ruleset waits for a result that will not come.

beats.text: Predicting a pull request path filter with a two-dot diff. Root cause: for pull requests the comparison is three dots, from the merge base; two dots include what changed on the base branch.
beats.tele: Predicting a pull request path filter with a two-dot diff. Root cause: for pull requests the comparison is three dots, from the merge base; two dots include what changed on the base branch.

beats.text: An if with text outside the expression wrapper. Root cause: the whole value becomes a non-empty string, which is truthy, so the condition is always true.
beats.tele: An `if` with text outside the expression wrapper. Root cause: the whole value becomes a non-empty string, which is truthy, so the condition is always true.

beats.text: A typing error in steps.<id>.outputs. Root cause: a property that does not exist evaluates to an empty string, without an error.
beats.tele: A typing error in `steps.<id>.outputs`. Root cause: a property that does not exist evaluates to an empty string, without an error.

beats.text: Expecting a secret in a fork pull request, or testing secrets in if. Root cause: secrets are not passed to workflows triggered from forks, and the secrets context is not available in if.
beats.tele: Expecting a secret in a fork pull request, or testing `secrets` in `if`. Root cause: secrets are not passed to workflows triggered from forks, and the `secrets` context is not available in `if`.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. A platform team runs a nightly evaluation with schedule. An engineer improves the evaluation workflow on a feature branch and waits for the night to see the result. In the morning the run has used the old workflow, and the engineer suspects a cache.

beats.text: Read the table. For schedule, the commit is the last commit on the default branch and the ref is the default branch. A scheduled run knows nothing about a feature branch. To try the changed workflow before merging, the engineer needs an event that's about a chosen ref.

says: The other four: workflow_call, workflow_run, merge_group and release
Three families: a specific commit, the default branch, the ref a person chose
schedule: the default branch. workflow_dispatch: the ref a person chose

beats.text: That is workflow_dispatch, with its own condition: it works only if the workflow file exists on the default branch. So the first version of a manually started workflow has to be merged before it can be started by hand from any branch at all.
beats.tele: That is `workflow_dispatch`, with its own condition: it works only if the workflow file exists on the default branch. So the first version of a manually started workflow has to be merged before it can be started by hand from any branch at all.

beats.text: Answer out loud first. A strong answer goes event by event and keeps the two questions separate, because they have different answers for some events. For pull_request it names the commit exactly and says why it isn't the branch tip. It mentions the condition attached to workflow_dispatch. The follow-up is about a pull request that edits its own workflow to remove a test: say whether the edited file runs, and then what that implies about who may change workflow files and what a required check can and can't guarantee.
